newsitem.title: USA: Support grows for Wisconsin bond audit.
newsitem.headline: Support grows for Wisconsin bond audit.

text.p: A key Wisconsin lawmaker said Wednesday she would push for an audit of state bond issues in the wake of revelations that a former aide to the governor received fees from groups receiving campaign contributions from bond underwriters.

The Republican co-chairman of the Wisconsin Legislative Joint Audit Committee, Rep. Mary Lazich, R-New Berlin, said she would seek the audit after hearing that the former top aide to Gov. Tommy Thompson was paid consulting fees from Republican political organizations that received contributions from Wall Street bond underwriting firms.

The audit was requested by State Rep. Spencer Black, D-Madison, who had asked the Legislative Audit Bureau to examine whether any of the contributing firms received preferential treatment when it came to the selection of underwriters.

"I think it's important for the people of the state of Wisconsin and across the nation to know the integrity of the institution is intact and there is not any inappropriate activity going on," Lazich said, adding that the audit should be placed on the fast track.

She was reportedly the first Republican to call for an investigation into local newspapers reports that James Klauser, who served as secretary of the state's Department of Administration up until December, received at least $114,000 from the Republican National State Elections Committee for consulting work between 1993 and 1996.
The Milwaukee Journal Sentinal has reported that Goldman, Sachs & Co., Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, Lehman Brothers, and Bear Stearns & Co contributed thousands of dollars to the elections committee.
Meanwhile, State Sen. Robert Wirch, D-Kenosha, the audit committee's other co-chairman, said Wednesday he was undecided on calling for an audit of bond issues.
He said he was still awaiting word on his request to the Wisconsin Attorney General's Office to launch a probe of possible Ethics of Campaign Finance Law violations.
"I clearly believe there should be a thorough investigation of the allegations," Wirch said, adding that he believed such an investigation should be done by the attorney general.
He also said that other lawmakers had raised concerns that the bond issue audit would displace other scheduled audits or that the matter could get politicized.

Klauser, who oversaw much of the state's bond issuance, has denied allegations of impropriety, claiming the charges were "all political." He has declined to verify any of the information contained in the newspaper reports.

Scott Hogenson, a spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said Klauser did general political consultant work for the committee for three months at the end of 1996, but had done most of his consultant work for the Republican Governor's Association.

Hogenson said he could not confirm whether any money from the Wall Street firms was placed in the state elections committee fund. However, he pointed out that money in that fund was not earmarked for any specific purpose. Instead it went to support entities such as the governor's association and local races throughout the nation, he said.
"A lot of large corporate constributions land up in the state elections account," he said, adding that the Wall Street firms' money could have been used anywhere.
Hogenson said that Klauser's role as a consultant was fully disclosed in campaign financing reports.
